questions.title: Not a muscle of facial expression
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a muscle of facial expression?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The frontal belly of occipitofrontalis is a genuine muscle of facial expression, supplied by the facial nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Orbicularis oculi is a genuine muscle of facial expression, closing the eye.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Platysma is a genuine muscle of facial expression, developing with the other facial muscles from the second pharyngeal arch and supplied by the facial nerve's cervical branch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Buccinator is a genuine muscle of facial expression, despite its role in chewing.
explanations.E: Correct. Temporalis is a muscle of mastication, developing from the first pharyngeal arch and supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), unlike the true muscles of facial expression, which all develop from the second pharyngeal arch and are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII). This different embryological origin and nerve supply is exactly what separates the muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoids) from the muscles of facial expression. Temporalis elevates and retracts the mandible during chewing, an action unrelated to facial expression.

questions.learning_objective: Identify temporalis as a muscle of mastication (first arch, trigeminal), not a muscle of facial expression.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.title: Infection from the dangerous area of the face
questions.question: Infection from dangerous area of face may be transmitted to the following venous sinus:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superior petrosal sinus is not the sinus classically linked to facial infection spread; it drains the cavernous sinus toward the transverse sinus, further along the venous pathway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The sigmoid sinus continues as the internal jugular vein and is not the classic destination for dangerous-area facial infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The inferior sagittal sinus runs along the free margin of the falx cerebri and has no direct connection to facial venous drainage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior sagittal sinus runs along the vault of the skull and has no direct connection to facial venous drainage.
explanations.E: Correct. The "dangerous area" of the face is the triangular region around the nose and upper lip, between the two anterior facial veins, so named because it drains via valveless veins, the facial vein to the deep facial vein to the pterygoid venous plexus to emissary veins, and via the ophthalmic veins, directly into the cavernous sinus. Because these facial veins lack valves, infection (for example from a squeezed nasal or upper-lip pimple) can spread backward into the cavernous sinus, causing potentially fatal cavernous sinus thrombosis. This is the classic clinical reason facial infections in this triangle are treated with particular caution.

questions.learning_objective: State that infection from the dangerous area of the face can spread via valveless facial veins to the cavernous sinus.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.title: Not true regarding buccinator
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT true regarding the buccinator?

options.A: It is a muscle of mastication.
options.B: It is innervated by the facial nerve.
options.C: It presses the cheek against the molar teeth to assist in chewing.
options.D: It expels air from the oral cavity.
options.E: It draws the mouth to one side when acting unilaterally.

explanations.A: Correct. Buccinator is, despite its role in chewing, classified as a muscle of facial expression, not a muscle of mastication: it develops from the second pharyngeal arch and is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), unlike the true muscles of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoids), which develop from the first arch and are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3). The statement that it "is a muscle of mastication" is therefore the false one among these options. All of buccinator's listed actions (pressing the cheek against the molars, expelling air, drawing the mouth to one side) are true.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This statement is true: buccinator is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, consistent with its facial-expression classification.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This statement is true: buccinator presses the cheek against the molar teeth, keeping food between the teeth during chewing and preventing it from pooling in the vestibule of the mouth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This statement is true: buccinator can expel air forcibly from the oral cavity, the action used in playing wind instruments (sometimes nicknamed the "trumpeter's muscle").
explanations.E: Incorrect. This statement is true: unilateral buccinator contraction draws the angle of the mouth to that side.

questions.learning_objective: State that buccinator is classified as a muscle of facial expression (facial nerve), not a muscle of mastication, despite its role in chewing.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.title: Plane of movement of the scalp
questions.question: Plane of Movement of the scalp is between:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The skin is firmly bound to the epicranial aponeurosis by the dense connective tissue layer between them, so there is no free plane of movement here; the two move together as a unit.
explanations.B: Correct. The scalp's five layers (Skin, dense subcutaneous Connective tissue, epicranial Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium) move as two functional units: the outer three layers (skin, connective tissue, aponeurosis) are firmly bound together and glide as a single unit over the pericranium, with the fourth layer, loose areolar tissue, acting as the plane of movement between the aponeurosis above and the pericranium below. This is the same loose areolar layer classically described as the "danger area" of the scalp, since it also allows blood or infection to spread widely. The scalp's mobility, for example when wrinkling the forehead, occurs through this aponeurosis-to-pericranium gliding plane.
explanations.C: Incorrect. There is no free gliding plane between the skin and its own subcutaneous fat; they are bound together as part of the same outer scalp unit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pericranium is the periosteum of the skull and is directly applied to bone; there is no significant gliding movement between them under normal circumstances.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The scalp does move, most obviously when the underlying occipitofrontalis muscle contracts to wrinkle the forehead or move the scalp backward.

questions.learning_objective: State that the scalp's plane of movement lies between the epicranial aponeurosis and the pericranium, within the loose areolar layer.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.title: Nerve supply behind the auricle
questions.question: The scalp is:

options.A: Supplied by the great auricular nerve in front of the auricle.
options.B: Supplied by the supratrochlear and supraobital arteries branches of the facial artery.
options.C: Supplied posteriorly by the greater occipital nerve from the ventral ramus of C2.
options.D: Supplied behind the auricle by the lesser occipital nerve from the ventral ramus of C2.
options.E: Drained by supratrochlear and supraorbital veins, which unite to form the superior ophthalmic vein.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The great auricular nerve, a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3), supplies the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible and the auricle itself, not the scalp in front of the auricle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The supratrochlear and supraorbital arteries are branches of the ophthalmic artery (via the internal carotid), not the facial artery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The greater occipital nerve does supply the posterior scalp, but it is the dorsal (posterior), not ventral, ramus of the second cervical spinal nerve (C2) that gives rise to it.
explanations.D: Correct. The lesser occipital nerve, a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus arising from the ventral ramus of C2 (with a C3 contribution), ascends behind the auricle to supply the scalp in this region, complementing the greater occipital nerve (posterior scalp, from the dorsal ramus of C2) and the great auricular nerve (over the auricle and angle of mandible, also ventral rami of C2-C3). This anterior/posterior, ventral/dorsal ramus distribution is a common source of confusion and a frequent exam point.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The supratrochlear and supraorbital veins unite at the medial angle of the eye to form the (anterior) facial vein, not the superior ophthalmic vein; the superior ophthalmic vein is instead the route by which the facial vein connects onward to the cavernous sinus.

questions.learning_objective: State that the scalp behind the auricle is supplied by the lesser occipital nerve, from the ventral ramus of C2.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.title: Emissary veins and infection spread from the scalp
questions.question: Choose one correct statement regarding the scalp:

options.A: Its wounds gape if superficial to aponeurosis.
options.B: Its blood vessels and nerves lie in the loose areolar connective tissue layer.
options.C: Its wounds do not bleed easily.
options.D: Bleeding beneath the periosteum usually extends under its whole extent.
options.E: Its infections can spread through emissary veins to cranial cavity.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Scalp wounds gape when they cut through the epicranial aponeurosis (deep to it, not merely superficial to it), because the aponeurosis's elastic fibres retract the wound edges once it is divided.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The scalp's blood vessels and cutaneous nerves run in the second (dense connective tissue) layer, not the fourth (loose areolar) layer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Scalp wounds bleed profusely, not sparingly, because vessels in the dense connective tissue layer are tethered open by fibrous septa and cannot easily retract or constrict.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Subperiosteal (subpericranial) bleeding is limited by the periosteum's firm attachment at the suture lines, so it stays confined to the boundary of one skull bone, unlike bleeding in the loose areolar layer, which can spread freely across the whole scalp.
explanations.E: Correct. Emissary veins are valveless veins that pass through small skull foramina (including the parietal foramen and, further afield, the foramen ovale and foramen lacerum), connecting the scalp's extracranial veins directly to the intracranial dural venous sinuses. Because they are valveless, infection in the scalp can travel along them inward to the cranial cavity, producing intracranial complications such as sinus thrombosis or meningitis. This is the same valveless-vein mechanism, applied to the scalp rather than the face, as the dangerous-area-of-the-face fact tested elsewhere in this lecture set.

questions.learning_objective: State that scalp infections can spread intracranially via valveless emissary veins.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.title: Nerve supplying the vertex of the scalp
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the vertex of the scalp:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The greater occipital nerve supplies the posterior scalp, behind the vertex, not the vertex itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The third occipital nerve supplies a small area near the nape of the neck, well posterior to the vertex.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the scalp above and in front of the ear (the temporal region), lateral to the vertex.
explanations.D: Correct. This source's own printed key names the supraorbital nerve, a terminal branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1), as reaching back as far as the vertex of the scalp, continuing the anterior-to-posterior supply pattern from the forehead. The supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves together supply the scalp anterior to the auricle, extending from the forehead back toward the vertex, before the auriculotemporal (laterally) and the occipital nerves (posteriorly) take over further back.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The supratrochlear nerve supplies a more medial strip of the forehead and anterior scalp, close to the midline, rather than specifically the vertex.

questions.learning_objective: State this source's printed answer for the nerve reaching the vertex of the scalp (supraorbital nerve).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.author_notes: Kept per printed key. Standard teaching more often describes the vertex as roughly the watershed between the anterior (supraorbital/supratrochlear), lateral (auriculotemporal) and posterior (greater occipital) territories rather than assigning it cleanly to one nerve; the supraorbital nerve is nonetheless the closest of these three to the vertex along the anterior-posterior scalp sequence, and no other page of this source states a conflicting answer, so this is a doubt rather than a same-source contradiction.

questions.title: Nerve supply of orbicularis oculi
questions.question: The orbicularis oculi is innervated by the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The oculomotor nerve (CN III) supplies most of the extraocular muscles and levator palpebrae superioris, not orbicularis oculi.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies only superior oblique, not orbicularis oculi.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The trigeminal nerve (CN V) provides sensory supply to the eyelids, not the motor supply that closes them.
explanations.D: Correct. Orbicularis oculi is a muscle of facial expression, a second-pharyngeal-arch derivative like all the other facial muscles, and receives its motor supply from the temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII). Its three parts, orbital, palpebral and lacrimal, all share this same facial nerve innervation, even though they perform different specific actions (firm protective closure, gentle blinking closure, and tear drainage respectively). This is the same facial-nerve rule that governs every other muscle of facial expression, including buccinator and occipitofrontalis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cervical plexus supplies platysma (via its cervical branch relationship with the facial nerve) and cutaneous branches to the neck and scalp, not orbicularis oculi.

questions.learning_objective: State that orbicularis oculi is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.68

questions.title: Cause of gaping in facial wounds
questions.question: The most important factor responsible for gaping of the facial wounds is the …….

options.A: thick and elastic nature of the skin.
options.B: cutaneous attachment of the facial muscles.
options.E: bone attachment of the facial muscles.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Facial skin is thin, not thick, and its elasticity is not the main factor behind wound gaping; the muscle attachment pattern is.
explanations.B: Correct. Unlike muscles elsewhere in the body, which typically attach to bone at both ends, the muscles of facial expression are unusual in taking origin from bone or fascia but inserting directly into the skin (cutaneous insertion). Because contraction of these muscles pulls directly on the skin along specific lines, a wound that crosses those lines of pull is actively pulled apart (gapes) by ongoing muscle tone and movement, unlike a wound running parallel to them. This cutaneous attachment is the anatomical reason facial lacerations are planned and closed along natural skin-crease lines whenever possible.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superficial fascia's looseness affects how easily skin can be undermined surgically, but it is not the principal reason facial wounds gape.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deep fascia is in fact largely absent in the face (unlike the limbs, where it is thick), but this absence is not itself the direct cause of wound gaping; the cutaneous muscle attachment is.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This describes ordinary skeletal muscles elsewhere in the body, not the facial muscles, which are distinctive precisely because they insert into skin rather than bone.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cutaneous insertion of the facial muscles is the main reason facial wounds gape.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.title: Buccinator paralysis and food accumulation
questions.question: Paralysis of which muscle lead to accumulation of food in the vestibule of the mouth?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Temporalis is a muscle of mastication that elevates and retracts the mandible; its paralysis affects chewing power and jaw closure, not cheek tone.
explanations.B: Correct. Buccinator normally presses the cheek inward against the molar teeth during chewing, keeping food positioned on the occlusal surfaces and preventing it from pooling between the cheek and gums (the vestibule). When buccinator is paralysed, as in a facial nerve palsy, this cheek support is lost, and food characteristically accumulates in the vestibule of the mouth, alongside drooling from loss of oral competence. This food-pocketing sign is a classic bedside clue to facial nerve dysfunction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Masseter is a muscle of mastication that elevates the mandible for biting force; its paralysis weakens the bite, not cheek tone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris paralysis affects the lips' ability to close the mouth and purse, not the cheek's ability to keep food on the teeth.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Medial pterygoid is a muscle of mastication contributing to mandibular elevation and side-to-side grinding movements, not cheek tone.

questions.learning_objective: State that buccinator paralysis (facial nerve injury) leads to food accumulating in the vestibule of the mouth.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.title: Embryological origin of the facial muscles
questions.question: The muscles of the facial expression………

options.A: receive motor supply from the trigeminal nerve.
options.C: originates from the connective tissue of the face.
options.D: are derived from the mesoderm of the pharyngeal arches.
options.E: inserted in the bones surround openings of the face.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the trigeminal nerve, which instead supplies the muscles of mastication and carries facial sensation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The muscles of facial expression move the skin and soft tissue of the face, producing expressions; they do not move the bony facial skeleton itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Skeletal muscle, including the facial muscles, develops from mesoderm, not from connective tissue.
explanations.D: Correct. All the muscles of facial expression develop from the mesoderm of the second pharyngeal (hyoid) arch, which is also why they share a single motor nerve supply, the facial nerve, the nerve of the second arch. This shared embryological origin explains several of this lecture's other facts: the facial nerve's five terminal branches supply every one of these muscles, and their unusual cutaneous (skin) rather than bony insertion is a related developmental feature.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Unlike ordinary skeletal muscles, the muscles of facial expression insert into the skin around the openings of the face (eyes, nose, mouth, ears), not into the surrounding bones; this cutaneous insertion is exactly what makes facial wounds prone to gaping.

questions.learning_objective: State that the muscles of facial expression are derived from second pharyngeal arch mesoderm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.author_notes: Main concept reused from the Alexandria AU-MED-203 lane's own concept (CON-NEU-BBDC83EF719120); see this lane's pending-live overlay. questions.title: The modiolus and buccinator
questions.question: The modulus is an anatomical structure related to which muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Temporalis is a muscle of mastication with no direct relationship to the modiolus.
explanations.B: Correct. The modiolus is a fibromuscular node at the corner (angle) of the mouth where several muscles of facial expression interlace and decussate, including buccinator, orbicularis oris and the muscles radiating from around the mouth. Buccinator's own fibres are a major contributor: its middle fibres decussate (cross over) as they pass forward to help form the modiolus, which is why the modiolus is classically associated specifically with buccinator among the answer choices here. This structure gives the corner of the mouth its firmness and mobility.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Masseter is a muscle of mastication attaching to the mandible and zygomatic arch, not related to the modiolus at the corner of the mouth.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris does contribute fibres to the modiolus, but the modiolus is more specifically taught, and tested by this source, in relation to buccinator's decussating fibres.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Medial pterygoid is a muscle of mastication deep to the mandible, unrelated to the modiolus.

questions.learning_objective: State that the modiolus is related to buccinator, whose middle fibres decussate to help form it.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.author_notes: Shares its main concept with q03 (buccinator classification); the modiolus/decussation detail itself is developed further in q23 ("modiolus represents the site of"), the more specific version of this same fact.

questions.title: Emissary veins and the loose areolar layer
questions.question: Emissary veins in the scalp are content of which scalp layer?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The skin is the outermost, avascular-of-emissary-veins layer, carrying only the fine cutaneous vessels and hair follicles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The second (dense connective tissue) layer carries the scalp's main arteries, veins and cutaneous nerves, but this is a different set of vessels from the emissary veins, which instead traverse the fourth layer.
explanations.C: Correct. The fourth scalp layer, loose areolar tissue, contains a few small arteries but is most notable for carrying the emissary veins, valveless veins that connect this layer's venous plexus directly to the intracranial dural venous sinuses through small skull foramina. Because this layer is also the plane along which the scalp's outer three layers glide over the pericranium, it is the same "danger area" through which blood, pus or infection can spread widely across the scalp and, via these very emissary veins, into the cranial cavity. This dual role, movement plane and emissary vein content, is why the loose areolar layer carries particular clinical importance.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The epicranial aponeurosis is a tough fibrous sheet connecting the two bellies of occipitofrontalis; it does not itself carry emissary veins.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The pericranium is the periosteum of the skull, the innermost scalp layer; it does not itself carry emissary veins, though the veins pass through the bone deep to it.

questions.learning_objective: State that emissary veins are carried in the loose areolar (fourth) layer of the scalp.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.title: Lateral extent of the scalp
questions.question: The scalp extends laterally to the……

explanations.A: Incorrect. The inferior temporal line marks the origin of temporalis further down the skull, below where the scalp's own lateral extent is defined.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior nuchal line marks part of the scalp's posterior boundary, not its lateral boundary.
explanations.C: Correct. The scalp is conventionally defined as extending from the eyebrows anteriorly to the superior nuchal line posteriorly, and laterally on each side down to the superior temporal line, the curved ridge on the side of the skull that marks the upper attachment of the temporal fascia. Below the superior temporal line, the temporal region and its own distinct fascia and fat pad take over. This lateral boundary complements the scalp's anterior boundary at the eyebrows, tested elsewhere in this lecture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inferior nuchal line is a lower posterior skull landmark, not the scalp's lateral boundary.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The zygomatic arch lies well below and lateral to the scalp proper, at the level of the face rather than the scalp's own boundary line.

questions.learning_objective: State that the scalp extends laterally to the superior temporal line.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.title: Occipitofrontalis and forehead corrugation
questions.question: Paralysis of which muscle lead to loss of corrugation of the forehead?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Temporalis is a muscle of mastication with no role in wrinkling the forehead.
explanations.B: Correct. Occipitofrontalis has two bellies joined by the epicranial aponeurosis: the occipital belly, arising from the occipital bone, and the frontal belly, which has no bony origin and instead inserts into the skin of the eyebrows and forehead. Contraction of the frontal belly raises the eyebrows and produces the transverse skin folds (corrugation) of the forehead, the expression of surprise. When the facial nerve is injured, this belly is paralysed and forehead corrugation is lost on the affected side, a key bedside sign distinguishing a facial nerve palsy from other causes of facial weakness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Masseter is a muscle of mastication with no role in wrinkling the forehead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris closes and purses the lips; it has no role in forehead wrinkling.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Medial pterygoid is a muscle of mastication with no role in wrinkling the forehead.

questions.learning_objective: State that occipitofrontalis's frontal belly produces forehead corrugation, lost when it is paralysed.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.title: Muscle draining tears
questions.question: Drainage of tears is facilitated by which muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Temporalis is a muscle of mastication with no role in tear drainage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Buccinator supports the cheek during chewing; it has no role in tear drainage.
explanations.C: Correct. Orbicularis oculi has three parts: orbital (firm, protective closure), palpebral (gentle, blinking closure), and lacrimal. The lacrimal part arises from the posterior lacrimal crest and encircles the lacrimal sac; its contraction with each blink compresses and dilates the lacrimal sac in sequence, actively pumping tears from the lacrimal punctum and canaliculi into the sac and onward into the nasolacrimal duct. This lacrimal-part pumping action is what makes orbicularis oculi, rather than any nearby muscle, responsible for facilitating tear drainage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Masseter is a muscle of mastication with no role in tear drainage.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris closes and purses the lips; it has no role in tear drainage.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi facilitates tear drainage by pumping the lacrimal sac.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.69

questions.title: Backward movement of the scalp
questions.question: The backward movement of the skin of the scalp is the function of……..

explanations.A: Incorrect. Platysma is a neck muscle that tenses the skin of the neck and depresses the mandible/lower lip; it does not move the scalp.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Buccinator supports the cheek during chewing; it has no role in moving the scalp.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris closes and purses the lips; it has no role in moving the scalp.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids; it has no role in moving the scalp.
explanations.E: Correct. Occipitofrontalis's two bellies act in sequence on the loosely mobile scalp: the frontal belly pulls the scalp forward and raises the eyebrows, wrinkling the forehead, while the occipital belly, anchored to the occipital bone and mastoid process, pulls the scalp backward. Both bellies act on the epicranial aponeurosis, sliding the outer three scalp layers over the pericranium along the loose areolar plane. The occipital belly's backward pull is therefore the answer to this specific direction of scalp movement, complementing the frontal belly's forward-pulling, corrugating action tested elsewhere in this lecture.

questions.learning_objective: State that the occipital belly of occipitofrontalis pulls the scalp backward.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.title: Buccinator's attachments
questions.question: The Buccinator muscle…….

options.D: is attached to both maxilla and mandible.
options.E: is supplied by the trigeminal nerve.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Buccinator is classified as a muscle of facial expression, not a muscle of mastication, even though it assists chewing by supporting the cheek.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Buccinator's fibres blend with orbicularis oris at the modiolus (corner of the mouth), not with orbicularis oculi around the eye.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Buccinator's fibres run predominantly horizontally, sweeping backward from the lips to the pterygomandibular raphe, not vertically.
explanations.D: Correct. Buccinator arises from the outer surfaces of the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible, opposite the molar teeth, as well as from the pterygomandibular raphe, and its fibres sweep forward to blend with orbicularis oris at the modiolus. This bony attachment to both jaws, at the level of the molar teeth, is what allows buccinator to press the cheek firmly against the teeth during chewing. It is a defining structural fact about the muscle, distinct from its facial-nerve supply and facial-expression classification.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Buccinator is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), not the trigeminal nerve, consistent with its facial-expression classification.

questions.learning_objective: State that buccinator is attached to both the maxilla and mandible at the level of the molar teeth.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.title: Black eye and the loose areolar layer
questions.question: Bleeding in………. layer of the scalp can cause black eye.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bleeding confined to the skin does not track to the eyelids; it stays localised to the site of injury.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superficial fascia (dense connective tissue layer) is the layer where scalp bleeding is typically profuse but localised, tethered open by fibrous septa rather than tracking widely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Deep fascia is essentially absent in the scalp/face region and is not the layer implicated in black eye formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pericranium is the innermost scalp layer, directly on bone; subperiosteal bleeding here is confined to one bone by the suture attachments and does not track to the eyelids.
explanations.E: Correct. The loose areolar tissue is the fourth scalp layer, a plane of easy cleavage sitting between the aponeurosis above and the pericranium below, extending forward beneath the frontal belly of occipitofrontalis into continuity with the eyelids' own loose subcutaneous tissue. Bleeding or pus within this loose areolar layer can therefore track anteriorly and pool in the eyelids under gravity, producing a "black eye" (periorbital ecchymosis) even from a scalp injury well away from the orbit itself. This same layer is also the classic plane of traumatic scalp avulsion, for the same structural reason: it is a loosely bound, easily separated plane.

questions.learning_objective: State that bleeding within the scalp's loose areolar layer can track forward and cause a black eye.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.author_notes: The Alexandria AU-MED-203 lane's loose-areolar-layer concept (CON-NEU-C4B0A8489B265C) covers a related but distinct fact (that source's own divergent "vascular layer" labelling of the 4th layer), so kept only as a contextual concept rather than reused as the main concept; a new concept is minted for this source's own black-eye fact.

questions.title: Orbicularis oris and closing the mouth
questions.question: Inability to close the mouth is mostly caused by loss of function of which muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Temporalis is a muscle of mastication controlling jaw elevation, not lip closure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Buccinator supports the cheek during chewing; its paralysis causes food pocketing, not inability to close the mouth (lips).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Occipitofrontalis acts on the scalp and eyebrows, unrelated to closing the mouth.
explanations.D: Correct. Orbicularis oris is the circular sphincter muscle of the lips, formed largely from fibres of the surrounding facial muscles converging at the modiolus. Its contraction closes and purses the lips, essential for keeping the mouth sealed, controlling speech sounds requiring lip closure, and containing food and saliva. When it is paralysed, most typically in a facial nerve (CN VII) lesion, the lips cannot be closed properly, leading to drooling and difficulty with lip-dependent tasks such as whistling or blowing out the cheeks.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids, not the mouth.

questions.learning_objective: State that orbicularis oris is the sphincter muscle responsible for closing the mouth.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.title: Platysma and neck vein pressure
questions.question: The muscle which help to releases the atmospheric pressure of skin on neck veins is the ….

explanations.A: Correct. Platysma is a broad, thin sheet of muscle in the superficial fascia of the neck, a facial-expression muscle supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. By tensing the skin of the neck, platysma is described as reducing the compressive effect of atmospheric (external) pressure on the underlying superficial neck veins, helping to keep them from being flattened, which supports venous return through them. This function is distinct from platysma's more familiar role in depressing the mandible and pulling down the corners of the mouth.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Buccinator lies in the cheek and has no role in tensing the skin of the neck over its veins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Occipitofrontalis acts on the scalp and forehead, unrelated to the neck's superficial veins.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris closes the lips, unrelated to the neck's superficial veins.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids, unrelated to the neck's superficial veins.

questions.learning_objective: State that platysma tenses the skin of the neck, helping counteract atmospheric pressure on the superficial neck veins.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.title: Origin of the auriculotemporal nerve
questions.question: The auriculotemporal nerve arises from…….

explanations.A: Correct. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), typically arising by two roots that encircle the middle meningeal artery before reuniting. It passes behind the temporomandibular joint, alongside the superficial temporal vessels, to supply sensation to the auricle, external auditory meatus, tympanic membrane and the skin of the temporal region, as well as carrying postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the parotid gland. Its origin from V3 places it among the mandibular division's sensory branches, alongside the buccal, lingual and inferior alveolar nerves.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The maxillary nerve (V2) supplies the mid-face; it is not the parent nerve of the auriculotemporal nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The ophthalmic nerve (V1) supplies the forehead, scalp anterior to the vertex, and orbit; it is not the parent nerve of the auriculotemporal nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The facial nerve (CN VII) is a separate cranial nerve providing motor supply to facial expression muscles; the auriculotemporal nerve is a trigeminal (sensory), not facial, branch, though it does carry the facial nerve's parasympathetic fibres to the parotid via a communicating branch.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The buccal nerve is itself another branch of the mandibular division, a sibling branch of the auriculotemporal nerve, not its parent.

questions.learning_objective: State that the auriculotemporal nerve arises from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.title: Modiolus as a site of muscle decussation
questions.question: The modiolus represents the site of…..

options.A: Decussation of the middle fibers of buccinator.
options.B: Origin of upper fibers of buccinator.
options.C: Insertion of upper fibers of buccinator.
options.D: Origin of lower fibers of buccinator.
options.E: Insertion of upper fibers of buccinator.

explanations.A: Correct. The modiolus is a dense fibromuscular node at the corner of the mouth where several facial muscles converge and interlace. Buccinator's own contribution is distinctive: its middle fibres cross over (decussate) as they run forward from the pterygomandibular raphe, so fibres from the upper part of the muscle end up passing to the lower lip and fibres from the lower part end up passing to the upper lip, meeting and interlacing at the modiolus. This decussation is the specific structural fact this source is testing, distinct from simply naming which muscle relates to the modiolus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes an origin, but buccinator's fibres arise from the maxilla, mandible and pterygomandibular raphe, not from the modiolus itself; the modiolus is where fibres converge and cross, not where they originate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Buccinator's own fibres do not simply insert at the modiolus in an orderly upper-fibre pattern; the defining feature is that the middle fibres decussate there.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes an origin, which is not what the modiolus represents for buccinator's fibres.
explanations.E: Incorrect (duplicate of option C on this printed item). Buccinator's defining relationship to the modiolus is the decussation of its middle fibres, not a simple insertion of upper fibres.

questions.learning_objective: State that the modiolus is the site where buccinator's middle fibres decussate.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.author_notes: The printed item repeats "Insertion of upper fibers of buccinator" as both option C and option E; kept verbatim as printed rather than silently corrected.

questions.title: Closest branch of the ophthalmic division to the midline
questions.question: The closest branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve to the midline is the ……..

explanations.A: Correct. This source's own printed key names the supratrochlear nerve as the ophthalmic division branch closest to the midline. The ophthalmic division (V1) gives off, from medial to lateral across the upper face, the infratrochlear, supratrochlear, supraorbital and lacrimal nerves; the supratrochlear nerve exits just above the trochlea near the medial corner of the eye and supplies a strip of forehead close to the midline, making it, on this source's account, the branch nearest the midline among these named options.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The supraorbital nerve exits through the supraorbital notch or foramen, lateral to the supratrochlear nerve's exit point, and supplies a wider, more lateral strip of the forehead and scalp.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The infratrochlear nerve, not listed as this source's chosen answer, supplies the medial eyelids, conjunctiva and side of the nose near the medial canthus; many standard descriptions place it, rather than the supratrochlear nerve, closest to the midline, a divergence flagged rather than silently resolved here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The infraorbital nerve is a branch of the maxillary division (V2), not the ophthalmic division, supplying the lower eyelid, cheek and upper lip.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lacrimal nerve runs to the lacrimal gland at the lateral part of the orbit, the most laterally placed of the ophthalmic division's branches, not close to the midline.

questions.learning_objective: State this source's printed answer for the ophthalmic-division branch closest to the midline (supratrochlear nerve).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.author_notes: Kept per printed key. Many standard anatomy references instead describe the infratrochlear nerve, not the supratrochlear nerve, as the branch closest to the midline (nearest the medial canthus); this source's own p.71/p.75 content does not restate the fact in conflicting terms, so this is recorded as a doubt rather than a same-source contradiction.

questions.title: Origin of the external nasal nerve
questions.question: The external nasal nerve is a branch of ……

explanations.A: Correct. The external nasal nerve supplies sensation to the skin of the lower half of the nose (the dorsum and tip). It is the terminal cutaneous continuation of the anterior ethmoidal nerve, itself a branch of the nasociliary nerve, itself a branch of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1). At the divisional level tested by this source, the external nasal nerve therefore belongs to the ophthalmic division's chain of branches, even though its most immediate parent branch is the anterior ethmoidal nerve rather than the ophthalmic nerve directly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The maxillary nerve (V2) supplies the mid-face and upper lip via its own separate branches (infraorbital, nasal branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion), not the external nasal nerve specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The mandibular nerve (V3) supplies the lower face and jaw; it has no branch called the external nasal nerve.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The facial nerve (CN VII) provides motor, not sensory, supply to the face and has no external nasal branch.
explanations.E: Incorrect, though this is the external nasal nerve's own immediate parent branch rather than an unrelated option: the anterior ethmoidal nerve gives rise to the external nasal nerve as its terminal cutaneous branch, but this source's printed key names the ophthalmic nerve (the parent division) rather than the anterior ethmoidal nerve (the immediate parent branch).

questions.learning_objective: State that the external nasal nerve belongs to the ophthalmic division's branch chain, via the anterior ethmoidal nerve.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.70

questions.author_notes: Kept per printed key. The more anatomically precise immediate parent is the anterior ethmoidal nerve (itself of the nasociliary nerve, itself of the ophthalmic division); this source tests the divisional level rather than the immediate branch, which is a defensible simplification rather than a same-source contradiction.

questions.title: Buccal branch of the mandibular nerve
questions.question: The buccal branch of the mandibular nerve supplies……

explanations.A: Incorrect. Buccinator's motor supply comes from the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), a different nerve with the same name for a different division.
explanations.B: Correct. The buccal branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) is a purely sensory branch, supplying the skin and mucous membrane overlying buccinator (the cheek), distinct from the buccal branch of the facial nerve, which is purely motor and supplies the buccinator muscle itself. This same-named-but-different-nerve pairing, one sensory (trigeminal) and one motor (facial), both called "buccal branch," is a classic source of confusion and a frequent exam point.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The skin of the temple is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve, another branch of V3, not the buccal branch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The muscles of the temple (temporalis) are supplied by the deep temporal nerves, separate branches of V3, not the buccal branch, which is purely sensory.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The skin of the chin is supplied by the mental nerve, the terminal cutaneous branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), not the buccal branch.

questions.learning_objective: State that the buccal branch of the mandibular nerve is sensory, supplying skin over buccinator, unlike the (motor) buccal branch of the facial nerve.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.author_notes: Main concept reused from the Alexandria AU-MED-203 lane's own concept (CON-NEU-BA080161837F03), which already states this exact sensory/motor buccal-branch distinction; see this lane's pending-live overlay.

questions.title: Sensation over the angle of the mandible
questions.question: The skin over the angle of the mandible sends its sensations to the….

explanations.A: Correct. The great auricular nerve, a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus (C2-C3), ascends over sternocleidomastoid to supply the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible and parts of the auricle. Because this territory sits just below and behind the trigeminal nerve's own facial coverage, it is a classic trap: students expect a trigeminal branch here, but the angle of the mandible is cervical-plexus, not trigeminal, territory.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the temporal region and auricle above and in front of the ear, a different area from the angle of the mandible.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The infraorbital nerve supplies the lower eyelid, cheek and upper lip, well above the angle of the mandible.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The external nasal nerve supplies the lower half of the nose, unrelated to the angle of the mandible.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The mental nerve supplies the skin of the chin and lower lip, anterior to the angle of the mandible.

questions.learning_objective: State that the great auricular nerve (cervical plexus, C2-C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.author_notes: Main concept reused from the Alexandria AU-MED-203 lane's own great-auricular-nerve concept (CON-NEU-088E2369B06007); see this lane's pending-live overlay.

questions.title: Lymphatic drainage of the lower lip
questions.question: The lower lip drains its lymph to …….

explanations.A: Correct. The central part of the lower lip drains its lymph to the submental lymph nodes, which lie in the midline beneath the chin, between the anterior bellies of digastric. This is one of a set of standard region-to-node pairings for the face and scalp: the lateral parts of the lower lip and much of the rest of the face instead drain more toward the submandibular nodes, but the central lower lip's own classic pairing, and the one tested here, is with the submental group.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The submandibular nodes drain the lateral parts of both lips, the cheek and much of the rest of the face, but the central lower lip's classic teaching pairing is with the submental, not submandibular, group.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The preauricular nodes drain the forehead, temple and cheek, not the lower lip.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The postauricular nodes drain the posterior scalp behind the ear, not the lower lip.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp, not the lower lip.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lower lip drains its lymph to the submental lymph nodes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.title: Temporal branch of the facial nerve
questions.question: The temporal branch of the facial nerve supplies……..

explanations.A: Incorrect. Buccinator is supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, not the temporal branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Skin over buccinator is a sensory territory of the trigeminal nerve's own buccal branch, not a motor territory of the facial nerve's temporal branch.
explanations.C: Correct. The facial nerve exits the parotid gland and divides into five conventional terminal branches: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular and cervical. The temporal branch crosses the zygomatic arch to supply frontalis (the frontal belly of occipitofrontalis), the upper part of orbicularis oculi, and corrugator supercilii. Among the options given here, orbicularis oculi is the one it supplies, complementing the zygomatic branch, which supplies the lower part of orbicularis oculi from the other direction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The muscles of the temple (temporalis) are muscles of mastication, supplied by the trigeminal nerve's deep temporal branches, not the facial nerve.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The skin of the chin is a sensory (trigeminal, mental nerve) territory, not a facial-nerve motor territory, and is not supplied by the temporal branch in any case.

questions.learning_objective: State that the temporal branch of the facial nerve supplies orbicularis oculi (its upper part) among its targets.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.title: Lymphatic drainage of the anterior scalp
questions.question: The anterior part of the scalp drains its lymph in the ……. lymph nodes.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The postauricular (mastoid) nodes drain the scalp behind and above the ear, not its anterior part.
explanations.B: Correct. The scalp's superficial lymphatic drainage broadly follows an anterior-to-posterior division: the anterior part of the scalp (the forehead region) drains to the preauricular (parotid) nodes, in front of the ear, while the posterior part drains to the occipital and postauricular groups behind the ear. This anterior/preauricular pairing complements the cheek's drainage, also to the preauricular group, tested elsewhere in this lecture.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The submandibular nodes drain the central face, lips and anterior tongue, not the anterior scalp.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The deep cervical nodes are the final common pathway that all these superficial groups eventually drain into, not the first-order nodes draining the anterior scalp directly.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp, not its anterior part.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior scalp drains its lymph to the preauricular lymph nodes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.title: Lymphatic drainage of the most posterior scalp
questions.question: The most posterior part of the scalp drains its lymph to …….

explanations.A: Incorrect. The submental nodes drain the chin and central lower lip, at the opposite (anterior, inferior) end of the head from the posterior scalp.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The submandibular nodes drain the central face and lips, not the posterior scalp.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The preauricular nodes drain the anterior scalp and forehead, the opposite end of the scalp's anterior-posterior drainage divide.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The postauricular (mastoid) nodes drain the scalp immediately behind and above the ear, an intermediate zone between the vertex and the very back of the scalp, rather than its single most posterior part.
explanations.E: Correct. The occipital lymph nodes lie over the insertion of trapezius near the occipital region and receive lymph specifically from the most posterior part of the scalp, completing the scalp's overall anterior-to-posterior drainage sequence: preauricular (front), postauricular/mastoid (behind the ear), and occipital (the very back). This posterior-most territory is distinct from the area just behind the ear, which drains instead to the postauricular group.

questions.learning_objective: State that the most posterior part of the scalp drains its lymph to the occipital lymph nodes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.title: Lymphatic drainage of the cheek
questions.question: The cheek region drains its lymph to …….

explanations.A: Incorrect. The submental nodes drain the chin and central lower lip, not the cheek.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The submandibular nodes drain the central face, nose and lips more than the cheek proper.
explanations.C: Correct. The cheek region drains its lymph forward and upward to the preauricular (parotid) lymph nodes, in front of and just below the ear, the same first-order node group that receives drainage from the anterior scalp and forehead. This shared preauricular pathway for the cheek and the anterior scalp/forehead is why an infection in either region can present with tender preauricular lymphadenopathy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The postauricular nodes drain the scalp behind the ear, not the cheek.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp, not the cheek.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cheek drains its lymph to the preauricular lymph nodes, the same group draining the anterior scalp.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.title: Mandibular trigeminal pathology and the scalp
questions.question: The mandibular division of trigeminal nerve pathology would affect which part of the scalp?

options.C: The scalp in front of the ear

explanations.A: Incorrect. The forehead is supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves), not the mandibular division.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The area above the eyebrows is likewise ophthalmic-division territory, not mandibular.
explanations.C: Correct. The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve reaches the scalp indirectly through its auriculotemporal branch, which ascends alongside the superficial temporal vessels to supply the temporal region, the scalp immediately above and in front of the ear. Pathology affecting the mandibular division can therefore produce sensory loss over this specific strip of scalp, distinguishing it from the ophthalmic division's anterior scalp/forehead territory and the cervical plexus's posterior scalp/behind-the-ear territory.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The scalp behind the ear is supplied by the lesser occipital nerve, a cervical plexus (not trigeminal) branch.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The occiput (back of the scalp) is supplied by the greater and third occipital nerves, cervical (not trigeminal) branches.

questions.learning_objective: State that mandibular-division trigeminal pathology (via the auriculotemporal nerve) affects the scalp in front of the ear.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.title: Spinal nerve pathology and the scalp
questions.question: Spinal nerves pathology would affect which part of the scalp?

options.C: The scalp in front of the ear.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The forehead is supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal (cranial) nerve, not by cervical spinal nerves.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The temple is supplied by the auriculotemporal nerve, a trigeminal (mandibular division) branch, not by cervical spinal nerves.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The scalp in front of the ear is likewise trigeminal (auriculotemporal) territory, not cervical spinal nerve territory.
explanations.D: Correct. The scalp behind the ear and over the posterior skull is supplied by cutaneous branches of the upper cervical spinal nerves rather than the trigeminal (cranial) nerve: the lesser occipital nerve (ventral ramus of C2, behind the auricle), the great auricular nerve (ventral rami of C2-C3, over the auricle and angle of mandible) and the greater occipital nerve (dorsal ramus of C2, the posterior scalp/occiput). Pathology of these cervical spinal nerves would therefore selectively affect the scalp behind the ear, sparing the anterior scalp and face, which are trigeminal (cranial nerve) territory instead.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The eyebrows lie within the ophthalmic division's (cranial nerve) territory, not cervical spinal nerve territory.

questions.learning_objective: State that cervical spinal nerve pathology affects the scalp behind the ear, the cutaneous territory of the cervical plexus rather than the trigeminal nerve.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.71

questions.title: Anterior facial vein and the cavernous sinus
questions.question: The anterior facial vein is connected to the cavernous sinus through…..

explanations.A: Correct. The anterior facial vein begins at the medial angle of the eye by the union of the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins, and it communicates there with the superior ophthalmic vein, which in turn drains directly and without valves into the cavernous sinus. This anterior facial vein to (superior) ophthalmic vein to cavernous sinus route is exactly the pathway that allows infection from the "dangerous area" of the face (around the nose and upper lip) to spread intracranially and cause cavernous sinus thrombosis, the same clinical fact tested from a different angle earlier in this lecture set.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The common facial vein is formed lower down, by the union of the anterior facial vein with the anterior division of the posterior facial (retromandibular) vein, and drains into the internal jugular vein, not the cavernous sinus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The external jugular vein is formed by the union of the retromandibular vein's posterior division with the posterior auricular vein and drains into the subclavian vein, with no direct connection to the cavernous sinus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior facial (retromandibular) vein is a separate vessel formed within the parotid gland, not the route connecting the anterior facial vein to the cavernous sinus.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The subclavian vein lies at the root of the neck, several venous generations away from the cavernous sinus, with no direct connection.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.72

questions.author_notes: Main concept reused from the Alexandria AU-MED-203 lane's own concept (CON-NEU-818A4F14FD6378, "the superior ophthalmic vein links the facial vein to the cavernous sinus"); see this lane's pending-live overlay.

questions.title: Facial nerve palsy vignette
questions.question: Patient is unable to close his right eye with dropping of the right angle of his mouth, which nerve is affected in that case?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ophthalmic nerve is a purely sensory branch of the trigeminal nerve; its lesion would cause sensory loss over the forehead and eye, not weakness of eye closure or the mouth.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The maxillary nerve is a purely sensory branch of the trigeminal nerve, supplying the mid-face; its lesion would not cause motor weakness of the eyelid or mouth.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The great auricular nerve is a purely sensory cervical plexus branch supplying skin over the parotid and mandible angle; its lesion would not cause the described motor weakness.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The mandibular nerve carries both sensory fibres (to the lower face) and motor fibres to the muscles of mastication, not to orbicularis oculi or the muscles around the mouth.
explanations.E: Correct. Orbicularis oculi (closing the eye) and the muscles around the mouth, including orbicularis oris and the muscles pulling up the angle of the mouth, are all muscles of facial expression supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII). A facial nerve lesion on one side therefore produces exactly this combination: inability to close the eye on the affected side (loss of orbicularis oculi function) together with drooping of the same-side angle of the mouth (loss of the muscles supporting it), the classic presentation of a lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy such as Bell's palsy.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise inability to close the eye plus drooping of the mouth angle as a facial nerve (CN VII) lesion.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.74

questions.title: Origin of the supraorbital artery
questions.question: Supraorbital artery is a branch of which of the following arteries?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superficial temporal artery is a separate terminal branch of the external carotid, unrelated to the supraorbital artery's own origin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The maxillary artery is the other terminal branch of the external carotid, likewise unrelated to the supraorbital artery's origin.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The facial artery is another external carotid branch supplying the superficial face, not the parent vessel of the supraorbital artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The transverse facial artery is a small branch of the superficial temporal artery, unrelated to the supraorbital artery's origin.
explanations.E: Correct. The supraorbital artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery, itself a branch of the internal carotid artery, arising within the orbit before passing through the supraorbital notch or foramen to supply the forehead and anterior scalp. This is the arterial counterpart of the supraorbital nerve's own path and territory, and it illustrates the general anastomosis between the internal carotid's ophthalmic branches and the external carotid's facial/superficial temporal branches over the forehead and scalp.

questions.learning_objective: State that the supraorbital artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.75

questions.title: Anterior boundary of the scalp
questions.question: Which one of the following is the anterior boundary of the scalp?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The hairline is a variable, individual feature that does not define the scalp's fixed anatomical boundary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The root of the nose lies well below and medial to the scalp's own anterior boundary.
explanations.C: Correct. The scalp is conventionally defined as extending from the eyebrows anteriorly to the superior nuchal line posteriorly, with the superior temporal line marking its lateral extent on each side. The eyebrows therefore mark the fixed anterior boundary used in anatomical description, regardless of an individual's actual hairline, which lies further back and is not itself the boundary used to define the scalp as an anatomical region.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The upper eyelids lie below the eyebrows, well anterior to and outside the scalp's own boundary.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The (superior) nuchal line marks the scalp's posterior, not anterior, boundary.

questions.learning_objective: State that the eyebrows mark the scalp's anterior boundary.

questions.title: Cervical branch of the facial nerve and platysma
questions.question: Which of the following muscles in supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stylohyoid is supplied by a separate branch of the facial nerve arising within the parotid gland (before it divides into its five terminal branches), not the cervical branch.
explanations.B: Correct. The facial nerve's five conventional terminal branches, temporal, zygomatic, buccal, mandibular and cervical, fan out from the parotid gland in that order from top to bottom. The most inferior of these, the cervical branch, descends into the neck to supply platysma, the broad, thin sheet of facial-expression muscle that lies in the superficial fascia of the neck. This placement is consistent with platysma's own status as a facial-expression (second-arch, facial-nerve) muscle despite lying outside the face proper.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Orbicularis oris is supplied by the buccal and mandibular branches of the facial nerve, not the cervical branch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Orbicularis oculi is supplied by the temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve, not the cervical branch.

questions.learning_objective: State that the cervical branch of the facial nerve supplies platysma.

questions.title: Palpebral branch of the infraorbital nerve
questions.question: The palpebral branch of the infraorbital nerve supplies the …….

explanations.A: Incorrect. The upper lid is supplied by branches of the ophthalmic division (supraorbital, supratrochlear, infratrochlear, lacrimal nerves), not the infraorbital nerve.
explanations.B: Correct. The infraorbital nerve, the continuation of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) after it passes through the infraorbital foramen, gives off palpebral, nasal and superior labial branches as it fans out over the mid-face. Its palpebral branch supplies the lower lid, complementing its nasal branch (side of the nose) and superior labial branch (upper lip). This fan-out pattern is why a single nerve, the infraorbital, supplies three adjacent but distinct regions.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The upper lip is supplied by the infraorbital nerve's superior labial branch, a separate branch from the palpebral branch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lower lip is supplied by the mental nerve, a branch of the mandibular division (V3), not the infraorbital nerve.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The side of the nose is supplied by the infraorbital nerve's nasal branch, a separate branch from the palpebral branch.

questions.learning_objective: State that the palpebral branch of the infraorbital nerve supplies the lower lid.
